chunks: Thin bond wires carrying high current. The question: Bond wires are often very thin but sometimes may need to carry lots of current. How do you reconcile this?
A single bond wire is thinner than a hair, and one wire can safely carry only about an amp.
Power chips need many amps, so they use many wires side by side, shorter or thicker wires, or solid copper straps instead of wires.
The reason is heating, which grows with the square of the current. Sharing the current among several wires cuts the heat in each wire sharply.
Imagine cars leaving a stadium. One narrow lane gets jammed. Open six lanes and each lane carries only a sixth of the cars.
Wires work the same way, with one important difference the analogy cannot show: the heat in each wire falls much faster than the share of current, because heat grows with the square of the current.
Doubling the current cuts the time to melt by four. This is a lower bound on survival time because real wires also lose heat to their ends.
For surges shorter than about a millisecond it is a good guide; for steady current it is far too pessimistic.
Current: the flow of charge, measured in amps. Resistance: how strongly a wire resists the flow of current, in ohms.
I to the 2R heating: the power turned into heat is current squared times resistance. In parallel: several paths side by side, so the current splits among them. for bond wires.
Fusing: a wire melting, like a fuse, when too much current heats it.
A 25 µm gold wire, 3 mm long, has about 0. 149 ohms of resistance. At 1 amps it turns 1² times 0. 149 about 0. 15 watts into heat. Now suppose the chip must carry 3 amps.
One wire would heat at 3² times 0. 149 about 1. 3 watts, far too much for a hair-thin wire. Use six wires in parallel. Each carries 0. 5 amps and heats at only 0. 5² times 0.
149 about 0. 037 watts. The total loss is about 0. 22 watts, and the combined resistance is 0. 149 ÷ 6 about 25 milliohms (thousandths of an ohm).
The safe current of a real wire depends on its length, material and package, so use the vendor's rating. That is the whole idea.

"A single 25 micron bond wire only handles roughly an amp or so, so for high current you reconcile it by using many wires in parallel, because resistance drops as 1/n and heating per wire as 1/n squared.
You also make them short, use fatter copper or aluminum wire or ribbon, or replace them with copper clips or flip-chip bumps.
For vertical power MOSFETs the drain current uses the backside. The caveat is that parallel wires don't share perfectly, so you check sharing and thermals."
